case_analysis.focal_point: When does a public official’s management of a social-media account—especially blocking or deleting comments from a critic—constitute governmental (state) action that triggers First Amendment limits on viewpoint discrimination?
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (speech and viewpoint discrimination) as incorporated against state and local officials through the Fourteenth Amendment; and the related “state action” / “under color of law” inquiry under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (implicitly implicated by the parties and amici, and expressly referenced by the United States as a closely related question).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (Lindke) argues that Freed’s Facebook activity should be treated as state action because the account functioned as an instrument of official communication and governance: Freed used it to speak in his capacity as City Manager, to disseminate information about city operations and public issues, and to interact with constituents about matters within his authority. On that view, blocking Lindke and deleting his comments amounted to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination in a forum the official effectively operated for public discussion. Petitioner and supporting amici generally urge a functional test focusing on how the account is actually used (official announcements, constituent service, invocation of office, use of government resources/authority), warning that a purely “personal account” label would allow officials to evade constitutional obligations by conducting governmental communication through privately branded pages.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Freed) argues that no state action occurred because he owned and controlled the Facebook page as a personal account and did not use it to perform an official duty or exercise governmental authority; therefore, his moderation decisions (blocking/deleting) were private choices not attributable to the state. Respondent’s framing, reflected in the Question Presented, pushes a narrower rule: a government employee’s social-media activity becomes state action only when the employee uses the account to carry out a specific governmental duty or purports to act with the authority of the office (not merely because the employee is a public official discussing public issues). This approach seeks to preserve officials’ ability to maintain personal online spaces without automatically converting them into constitutionally regulated public forums.
key_precedents: Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021) (vacatur/mootness, but noted as illustrating the importance of the issue for officials’ social-media use)
Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump, 928 F.3d 226 (2d Cir. 2019), vacated as moot, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021) (President’s blocking users from Twitter as state action / public forum analysis)
Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922 (1982) (framework for attributing conduct to the state; state action / under-color-of-law relationship)
Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982) (state action standards; when private conduct is attributable to the state)
Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019) (limits on treating private entities/venues as state actors; state action and public forum concepts)
Davison v. Randall, 912 F.3d 666 (4th Cir. 2019) (official’s Facebook page; blocking as state action and forum-based viewpoint discrimination)
Garnier v. O’Connor-Ratcliff, 41 F.4th 1158 (9th Cir. 2022) (school board officials’ social-media pages; blocking as state action—one of the paired cases)
Lindke v. Freed, 37 F.4th 1199 (6th Cir. 2022) (the decision under review; Sixth Circuit’s approach to state action for officials’ social-media pages)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s “instrument of governance” warning is the best point for Petitioner: officials should not be able to launder official communications through a “personal” label and then exclude critics. But under Lugar and Blum the attribution inquiry remains act-specific, and their functional test risks collapsing into a status/subject-matter rule that treats private editorial moderation as state action whenever an official discusses government or engages constituents—precisely the sweep Halleck cautions against absent governmental control or an exercise (or pretense) of state-conferred authority. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on the nature of the act supplies the narrow limiting principle: the blocking/deletion must be tied to performing an official duty or to invoking official power, not merely to the account’s audience, appearance, or usefulness as a communication channel. I would therefore keep the holding narrow—leaving room for Davison/Knight-type cases where objective indicia show the account is operated as an official instrumentality—while affirming on this record because the required close nexus to governmental authority in the challenged moderation decision is missing.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “instrument of governance” theory most forcefully presses the anti-evasion concern, but it still does not satisfy Lugar/Blum’s act-specific requirement that the challenged exclusion be fairly attributable to state-conferred authority rather than to private control of a privately created account. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, we must look to the nature of the act—blocking/deleting—and ask whether the official exercised or purported to exercise governmental power in doing so; absent that nexus, the analysis collapses into a status-and-subject-matter rule incompatible with Jackson and Halleck’s caution against constitutionalizing private editorial choices. Davison/Knight (which Sotomayor and Jackson invoke) may illustrate harder cases where an account is operationally integrated with the office (staff administration, formal designation, or performance of an official duty), but those indicia are not established here in a way that ties the moderation decision to state authority. Under an originalist and textualist reading of § 1983’s “under color of” requirement and our state-action precedents, I would affirm for Respondent on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “instrument of governance” point is the strongest for Petitioner because it identifies a real risk of evasion when officials use interactive pages to communicate with constituents, but it still does not satisfy Lugar/Blum’s requirement of a close nexus between the State and the specific challenged act—here, blocking or deleting. Under my textualist and act-specific approach, the relevant question is whether the moderation decision was made by virtue of state-conferred authority or under the pretense of such authority; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, discussing official topics and inviting feedback on a privately controlled page is not itself an exercise of governmental power. Davison and the Knight line (which Sotomayor and Justice Jackson invoke) may involve stronger indicia of official operation (formal designation, staff use, institutional control), but adopting their broader functional test here risks collapsing the state-action boundary into a status/subject-matter rule and constitutionalizing private editorial control contrary to Halleck’s caution. I therefore remain with Respondent because the proposed “appearance-and-function” approach is insufficiently tethered to the authority element that § 1983 and our state-action cases demand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s act-specific, administrable “duty/authority” limiter rightly warns—under Lugar/Blum and Halleck—against collapsing state action into a status-plus-subject-matter test and constitutionalizing ordinary private editorial control. But their framing is too narrow for how officials actually wield power: when an officeholder objectively holds an interactive account out as a channel for official information and constituent access, the exclusion of critics is fairly attributable to the State because the challenged act (blocking) is inseparable from the official’s exercise of his public role in that forum-like space. Halleck cuts the other way here because it rejects treating the private platform as the state actor; my focus is the officeholder’s use of the account as an instrument of governance, which satisfies the “close nexus” inquiry without turning every personal page into state action. Justice Jackson’s emphasis on objective indicia of official use supplies the limiting principle Respondent seeks while still protecting vulnerable constituents’ access to and accountability from government actors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “instrument of governance” argument powerfully identifies an evasion risk—officials could relabel accounts as “personal” and then engage in viewpoint discrimination—but I do not think it satisfies Lugar/Blum’s act-specific nexus requirement unless the blocking decision itself is plausibly an exercise (or pretense) of state-conferred authority. Justice Jackson’s proposed “objective indicia” test helps, and it usefully incorporates Davison/Knight-like facts, but absent clearer indicia of governmental control, formal designation, staff operation, or performance of an official duty, it still trends toward a status-and-subject-matter proxy that Halleck warns against by constitutionalizing private editorial control on privately controlled property. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower, administrable line—tied to whether the moderation act invokes or purports to invoke governmental power—better preserves § 1983 coherence while still leaving room to find state action where an account is effectively operated as an official channel. On this record as framed, I remain with Respondent because the attribution showing seems insufficiently tethered to the specific challenged act of blocking/deleting.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (joined in part by Justice Jackson) offers the best counter: a functional “instrument of governance” test would deter evasion where officials route constituent services and official announcements through nominally “personal” accounts. But under Lugar and Blum, attribution is act-specific and demands a close nexus between the State and the particular exclusionary act; absent evidence that the blocking was done by virtue of (or in pretense of) state-conferred authority, function-and-appearance risks collapsing state action into a status/subject-matter inquiry. Halleck reinforces that we should not constitutionalize editorial control over privately controlled spaces merely because they are used for public debate, and the Davison/Knight line (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan note) is at most persuasive where there are tighter indicia of official control or duty—indicia missing on this record. I therefore remain with the Chief Justice’s administrable “duty/authority” rule and would affirm for Respondent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: a functional “instrument of governance” test is needed to prevent evasion when officials use ostensibly personal accounts for constituent access and official updates. But under Lugar and Blum, attribution is act-specific; as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, we need a close nexus between the State and the particular blocking/deletion decision, meaning the official must be exercising or purporting to exercise state-conferred authority in that act, not merely speaking about public matters in a space he controls. Davison and the (vacated) Knight Institute decision, which Sotomayor/Jackson cite, are informative where the account is integrated with official operations (staffing, formal designation, governmental control, duty-linked use), but they do not justify collapsing state action into a status-plus-subject-matter rule—especially given Halleck’s caution against constitutionalizing private editorial control on privately controlled property. I therefore remain with the narrower, more administrable rule keyed to actual or purported governmental authority, which addresses evasion without sweeping in ordinary personal-account moderation by public employees.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “instrument of governance” argument most squarely presses the evasion concern, but under Lugar and Blum the attribution inquiry remains act-specific: we must ask whether the blocking/deletion decision itself was taken by virtue (or pretense) of state-conferred authority, not merely because the account discussed official business or invited constituent engagement. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrable limiter—tying state action to the use of the account as an instrumentality of official power or to perform an official duty—better preserves the “under color of” requirement and avoids converting § 1983 into a status-plus-subject-matter rule. Justice Jackson’s proposal to use “objective indicia” (office identification, announcements, constituent-service interactions) is helpful as evidence, but without a showing that moderation purported to be an exercise of governmental power it still risks collapsing the nexus inquiry into appearance and function, contrary to Halleck’s warning against constitutionalizing private editorial control on private property. Davison and the vacated Knight decision underscore the practical problem in closer-to-official accounts, yet they do not supply a limiting principle consistent with our close-nexus precedents on this record as framed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s act-specific “duty/authority” limiter rightly invokes Lugar/Blum’s close-nexus requirement and Halleck’s warning against constitutionalizing private editorial control, but it is too cramped for the real-world way officials can deploy an interactive account as a practical channel of governance without a formal legal duty to do so. The key nexus is not whether state law expressly authorizes “blocking,” but whether the official has objectively held the account out as an office-linked conduit (official identification, announcements, and constituent-service routing) such that exclusion operates as a state-attributable denial of access to that channel—Lugar’s attribution inquiry looks to function and use, not formal duty labels. Justice Thomas’s concern about a status-and-subject-matter test is answered by an objective-indicia standard that cabins liability to accounts operationally used as office instruments, leaving genuinely personal pages outside § 1983. Because the practical consequences of respondents’ rule would invite evasion—officials can shift constituent access and accountability to “personal” pages and then viewpoint-discriminate with impunity—I remain with Petitioner under a procedurally fairness-oriented, pragmatic application of state-action doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the First Amendment applies only if the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State,” which requires more than a public official speaking about public issues on privately controlled property. Consistent with Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck and this Court’s reluctance to expand state-action doctrine, I would adopt a narrow, administrable rule: a public official’s moderation of a personal social-media account is state action only when the official uses that account to exercise (or purport to exercise) actual governmental authority—i.e., to carry out an official duty in a way that would reasonably be understood as the government itself speaking or acting. On this record and given the Sixth Circuit’s framing, treating Freed’s blocking/deletion decisions as private choices best preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding a sweeping constitutional rule that would convert many officials’ personal online spaces into regulated public forums. The proper remedy is a clarifying standard for future cases, but judgment here should be for Respondent because § 1983 liability cannot attach absent action “under color of” state law fairly attributable to the State.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment constrains only governmental action, and under § 1983 the relevant inquiry is whether the official “purports to act under” state authority such that the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 935 & n.18 (1982); West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42, 56 n.15 (1988). A public employee’s mere discussion of public affairs on a privately controlled social-media page does not itself constitute an exercise of governmental power; the account must be used to perform an actual official duty or to invoke the authority of the office in a way that makes the moderation decision an act “under color of” law. This narrower attribution rule also accords with our state-action cases’ insistence on a “close nexus” between the State and the specific challenged action, Jackson v. Metro. Edison Co., 419 U.S. 345, 351 (1974), and avoids converting private speech platforms into government forums contrary to the limits emphasized in Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The First Amendment constrains only governmental conduct, and § 1983 requires deprivation of a federal right “under color” of state law—i.e., conduct “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 937 (1982). Where an official controls a privately owned social-media account and moderates it without invoking or exercising governmental authority, the nexus to the State is too attenuated; treating ordinary discussion of public issues as state action would collapse the state-action line and invite pervasive judicial supervision of officials’ personal speech. Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019), counsels against broadening state-action/public-forum doctrines simply because a space is used for public expression. On this record and under a narrow, duty/authority-focused test, the blocking/deletion decisions are best understood as private conduct rather than action taken “under color” of law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A public official’s social-media moderation constitutes state action when, in function and appearance, the official uses the account as an instrument of governance—invoking the office, communicating official business, and soliciting or responding to constituent concerns within the official’s authority—so that the exclusion of critics is fairly attributable to the State under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co. and § 1983’s “under color of law” requirement. On that record, blocking and deleting comments because of their viewpoint is forbidden by the First Amendment once the official has effectively opened an interactive space for public discussion of governmental matters, as courts recognized in Davison v. Randall and the (vacated but instructive) Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump decisions. A purely formal “personal account” label cannot defeat constitutional scrutiny where the practical effect is to channel official communications through a privately branded page and then selectively silence disfavored speakers, particularly those seeking access to their government. The proper rule is a functional one that protects citizens’ access to officials’ chosen channels for official communication while leaving room for truly personal pages that are not used to perform or present official functions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The First Amendment limits Lindke invokes apply only to conduct “fairly attributable to the State,” and § 1983’s “under color of law” inquiry tracks that same state-action requirement. Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 929, 937 (1982). Where an official uses a privately owned social-media account, state action turns on whether the official is exercising (or purporting to exercise) authority conferred by state law—i.e., the nature of the act, not merely the speaker’s identity or the fact that the account discusses public issues—consistent with Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982), and Halleck’s insistence that private choices are not automatically constitutionalized. On this record and framing, treating Freed’s moderation of his personal Facebook page as state action absent a showing that he was carrying out an official duty or invoking official authority would be unworkable and overbroad, sweeping in ordinary personal speech by public employees and blurring the state/private line the Fourteenth Amendment presupposes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The First Amendment constrains only governmental conduct, and § 1983 likewise reaches deprivations committed “under color of” state law; under Lugar, conduct is fairly attributable to the State only when the challenged action is tied to the “exercise of some right or privilege created by the State” or the official’s use (or pretense) of governmental authority. A public employee’s discussion of public issues on a privately owned social-media page is not, without more, the exercise of a power “possessed by virtue of state law,” and Halleck cautions against converting private property and private editorial control into state action merely because it is used for public discussion. Absent a showing that Freed was performing an official duty through the account or invoking his office’s authority in moderating access, blocking and deleting comments remain private choices not attributable to the City. This rule respects the separation of powers by keeping courts from constitutionalizing every online interaction by government employees while still leaving room to find state action when an official actually wields governmental authority online.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The First Amendment, as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment and enforced via 42 U.S.C. § 1983, applies only to conduct that is fairly attributable to the State. Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the challenged deprivation must be caused by the exercise of a right or privilege created by the State or by a person for whom the State is responsible, and Halleck cautions against converting private property and private editorial control into state action absent a traditional, exclusive public function or governmental control. On this record, respondent’s privately owned and controlled Facebook page—created before taking office and not controlled or accessed by the City—does not, without more, show that his blocking/deletion decisions were made under color of law or pursuant to governmental authority rather than private account management. A narrower, workably administrable rule best preserves officials’ ability to maintain personal speech while still allowing liability when an official actually invokes or exercises governmental power through the account.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The First and Fourteenth Amendments constrain only governmental action, and § 1983 similarly requires conduct “under color of” state law; under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., attribution turns on whether the challenged deprivation is fairly attributable to the State, not merely on the defendant’s public employment. Consistent with Halleck and Blum, a public official’s use of a privately owned social-media account is state action only when the official is exercising governmental authority or performing an official duty through that account (i.e., invoking or purporting to wield the power of the office), not simply discussing public issues. On this record as framed, treating all such account moderation as state action would collapse the state-action inquiry into a status-based rule and would be methodologically inconsistent with the Court’s insistence that “the nature of the act performed” controls. Because the moderation decisions here are best understood as private choices absent a showing that Freed used the account as an instrument of official power, I would vote to affirm for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When an official uses a social-media account as an instrument of governance—invoking their office, conveying operational information, and engaging constituents on matters within their authority—their content-moderation decisions can be “fairly attributable to the State” under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 935–37 (1982), thus constituting action under color of law for § 1983 purposes. This functional approach respects the First Amendment’s anti–viewpoint-discrimination rule by preventing officials from evading constitutional constraints through a “personal account” label while still allowing genuinely private online activity to remain private, consistent with Halleck’s insistence on a disciplined state-action boundary. On these facts, blocking and deleting a critic’s comments in a space used for official communication and constituent interaction resembles the state action found in cases like Davison v. Randall, 912 F.3d 666 (4th Cir. 2019), and the practical consequences counsel a workable rule that incentivizes clear, fair procedures for public-facing moderation. Accordingly, the First Amendment applies once the official uses the account to perform or appear to perform official functions, and viewpoint-based exclusions in that governmental forum are unconstitutional.

case_analysis.focal_point: When a public official (or employee) blocks a user from a social-media account, under what circumstances does that action constitute “state action” (and thus trigger First Amendment constraints) rather than private conduct?
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (speech/retaliation and viewpoint discrimination principles) as incorporated against state and local officials through U.S. Const. amend. XIV; relatedly, the “under color of state law” requirement for 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (Lindke) argues that Freed’s management of his Facebook page—including blocking Lindke and deleting comments—should be treated as governmental (state) action because Freed used the account in ways tied to his public role (e.g., communicating with constituents about city matters, presenting himself as City Manager, and using the account as a channel for official information). On that view, the interactive space of the page functions like a forum the government has opened for public discussion, so excluding critics is unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Freed) argues that his Facebook page was personal property and his moderation decisions were private acts, not state action, because he did not operate the account pursuant to any governmental duty, nor did he exercise power made possible only by his office. Even if he occasionally posted about public issues, he contends that does not convert a privately controlled social-media account into an official government channel, and therefore the First Amendment (and § 1983) should not apply to his blocking/deletion decisions.
key_precedents: Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021) (mootness disposition; noted relevance of state-action issues in officials’ social-media use)
Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922 (1982) (state-action / 'under color of law' framework)
Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Assn., 531 U.S. 288 (2001) (tests for identifying state action, including entwinement)
Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982) (state-action limits; private decisions not attributable to the state absent sufficient governmental involvement)
Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019) (private entities and state action; operating a forum generally not a traditional exclusive public function)
Davison v. Randall, 912 F.3d 666 (4th Cir. 2019) (official’s Facebook page blocking as state action / First Amendment violation)
Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump, 928 F.3d 226 (2d Cir. 2019), vacated as moot, 141 S. Ct. 1220 (2021) (public forum analysis for official social-media accounts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that the blocking tool is a private platform privilege and Blum/Halleck demand more than “official-ish” speech—presses the need for a limiting principle, but it does not, in my view, defeat attribution under Lugar. Lugar’s inquiry is whether the specific exclusion is fairly attributable to the State; when, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, an official objectively holds an account out and uses it as an ongoing channel for official announcements and constituent interaction, the decision to exclude operates under the mantle of office in a government-facing interface even if the mechanics are privately supplied. Halleck remains satisfied because we are not converting the platform into a state actor or deeming social media a traditional public function; we are only treating the officeholder’s exclusion as state action in the narrow category of accounts functioning as an instrumentality of governance. A fact-bound rule keyed to objective indicia of official use answers the administrability and chilling concerns without letting officials evade First Amendment constraints by migrating official engagement to privately hosted accounts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s “instrument of office” theory (echoed by Justice Kagan) is the strongest argument for Petitioner, but it ultimately rests on self-presentation and audience expectations rather than on power “possessed by virtue of state law” as Lugar requires. Under Blum and Halleck, the relevant question is whether the specific deprivation—blocking—was enabled by state authority, coercion, or significant encouragement; here, as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the blocking tool is a private platform feature available to every user and not delegated, directed, or controlled by the State. Justice Sotomayor’s Brentwood-style “entwinement” framing usefully highlights an evasion risk, but entwinement in Brentwood is institutional and supervisory, not merely a practical blending of personal and official speech in a privately controlled space. I would leave open a different case with formal governmental designation or control of the account/moderation, but on this record § 1983’s “under color of” limitation is not met.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “instrument of office/held out” indicia test is the Petitioners’ strongest move because it tries to supply an administrable limit while capturing practical realities, but it still shifts the Lugar/Blum inquiry from state-conferred authority over the challenged deprivation to appearance and usage. Even accepting Justice Kagan’s functional attribution framing, the specific act—blocking—derives from a platform privilege “any user has,” with no delegation, duty, coercion, or governmental control over moderation, so it is not conduct “possessed by virtue of state law” or significantly encouraged by the State. Justice Sotomayor’s Brentwood entwinement concern identifies an evasion risk, yet Brentwood’s “pervasive entwinement” is structural and supervisory; here the asserted nexus is largely communicative, and Halleck cautions against collapsing private editorial control into state action. I therefore would reserve § 1983 liability for cases with clearer governmental designation or control of the account or access rules, which this record does not show.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Blum/Halleck objection is the sharpest: the block function is a private platform tool and we must not treat every “official-ish” account as state action. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Lugar’s attribution inquiry is functional and specific to the challenged exclusion: when an officeholder objectively holds an account out as an ongoing channel for official announcements and constituent engagement, the act of blocking in that government-facing space is done under color of law even if the platform supplies the mechanics. Halleck limits treating the platform as a state actor; it does not foreclose attributing the officeholder’s exclusion decision to the State where the account has become an instrumentality of governance, and Brentwood’s entwinement captures that practical integration without collapsing the boundary because Roberts’s objective-indicia approach cabins liability to accounts genuinely used as part of the office. The real-world consequence—denying critics equal access to a public-facing government communications channel—counsels against a rule that would invite easy evasion by routing official business through “private” accounts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point: under Lugar/Blum the “power” must be state-conferred, and the blocking tool is a private platform feature any user has, so audience perception alone cannot supply state action. But Lugar’s attribution inquiry is not limited to formal delegation; it asks whether this specific exclusion is fairly attributable to the State, and Chief Justice Roberts’s account-specific, objective-indicia approach supplies the needed tether by requiring that the official hold the account out and use it as an ongoing channel for official announcements and constituent engagement. On that narrower set of facts, the blocking operates under the mantle of office in a government-facing communicative instrument, without converting the platform into a state actor (addressing Halleck) or treating social media as a traditional public function. I therefore see the respondents’ formalism as underinclusive and too easily evaded, while Roberts’s limiting principle answers the administrability and chilling-speech concerns without diluting § 1983 into a vibes test.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s indicia-based “instrument of office” test (echoed by Justice Kagan) is the most serious argument for Petitioner because it offers an administrable limit and tracks real-world constituent reliance, but it still shifts the Lugar/Blum inquiry from state-conferred power over the specific deprivation to audience perception and self-presentation. Under Lugar, the question is whether the blocking was accomplished through authority “possessed by virtue of state law” or through state coercion/encouragement; here, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the power to block is a platform feature held by every private user, with no delegation, duty, or governmental control tethering that tool to state authority. Justice Sotomayor’s Brentwood entwinement concerns underscore an evasion risk, yet Brentwood’s “pervasive entwinement” is typically institutional and supervisory; on this record it would effectively collapse the state-action limit into a fact-bound “held out as official” test that Halleck cautions against. I would reserve a different case where law or policy formally designates the account as an official portal or subjects moderation to governmental direction, but these facts do not satisfy § 1983’s under-color-of-law requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “instrument of office” framing is the most serious challenge because it offers an administrable, objective-indicia limit while capturing how constituents experience these accounts; Justice Kagan similarly argues Lugar is not so formalistic about delegation. But under Lugar and Blum the attribution inquiry must remain tethered to state-conferred authority or meaningful state control over the specific deprivation, and here the blocking power is a platform-provided tool any private user wields, with no evidence of governmental duty, delegation, coercion, or supervisory policy governing moderation (as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize). Justice Sotomayor’s Brentwood entwinement concern flags an evasion risk, yet Brentwood’s “pervasive entwinement” is typically structural and institutional; treating self-presentation and audience expectations as enough would collapse the state-action boundary into a “held out” test and dilute Halleck’s warning against converting private control of speech spaces into state action. I would leave room for liability on a different record (formal designation as an official channel or government control over access/moderation), but this record does not satisfy § 1983’s under-color-of-law requirement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “instrument of office/held out” theory is the Petitioners’ best argument, but as Justice Gorsuch explains, Lugar and Blum tether attribution to whether the specific deprivation was effected through authority possessed by virtue of state law or through significant state involvement, not through self-presentation or audience understanding. Justice Kagan’s functional framing usefully separates platform state-actor questions (Halleck) from attribution, yet it still treats the private blocking tool—available to every user and exercised without delegation, duty, coercion, or governmental control—as if it were state-enabled power. Justice Sotomayor’s Brentwood entwinement concern highlights an evasion risk, but Brentwood’s “pervasive entwinement” is typically structural and supervisory, and here the record shows discretionary use of privately owned property rather than institutional integration over moderation decisions. On this record, the nexus between state authority and the blocking decision remains too attenuated to satisfy § 1983’s “under color of” requirement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that Blum/Halleck and Lugar require more than “official-ish” use because the blocking tool is a private platform privilege—does not, in my view, defeat attribution where the official has objectively converted the account into an ongoing channel for official announcements and constituent-service interaction. Under Lugar’s fair-attribution inquiry, the relevant question is whether the exclusion is bound up with the exercise of apparent governmental authority in a government-facing interface, not whether the technological mechanism is privately supplied; otherwise officials could practically evade viewpoint-neutral access simply by choosing a privately built communications conduit. Chief Justice Roberts’s indicia-based approach supplies the administrable limiting principle respondents demand, avoiding Halleck’s concern about transforming the platform into a state actor while still treating the officeholder’s exclusion decision, in an account functioning as an instrument of office, as under color of law. Justice Thomas is right to worry about mixed-use accounts, but requiring concrete, objective markers of official use (beyond title or political speech) cabins liability in a way consistent with procedural fairness and real-world consequences.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., § 1983’s “under color of law” requirement tracks the Fourteenth Amendment state-action inquiry and turns on whether the challenged conduct is “fairly attributable to the State,” including whether it was “made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with the authority of state law.” When an official uses a social-media account as an instrument of his office—holding it out as an official channel, using it to communicate governmental decisions or services, and invoking apparent authority to manage constituent interaction—blocking and comment-deletion are best understood as exercises of state-conferred authority rather than purely private choices. That approach is consistent with the limits emphasized in Blum v. Yaretsky and Halleck (not every private platform decision is state action), while still recognizing, as in Davison v. Randall, that an official’s control over an interactive space used for official communication can trigger First Amendment constraints against viewpoint discrimination. A narrow ruling should focus on the specific, account-specific indicia of official use and avoid a broad rule that every public official’s mixed-use account is state action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First and Fourteenth Amendments constrain only governmental conduct, and § 1983 likewise reaches only deprivations committed “under color of” state law; thus the dispositive question is whether the blocking is “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 937 (1982). On an originalist and textualist understanding, a public employee’s use of privately created and privately controlled social-media property does not become state action merely because he discusses public matters there; absent a showing that the official acted pursuant to an actual governmental duty or exercised authority made possible only by state law, the moderation decision remains private conduct under Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982). Halleck reinforces that merely providing a space for speech—even if functionally a forum—is not, without more, a traditional and exclusive public function attributable to the State. Manhattan Cmty. Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1983 and the First Amendment apply only when the challenged moderation decision is fairly attributable to the State—i.e., when the official “exercised power possessed by virtue of state law and made possible only because [he] is clothed with the authority of state law.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 937 (1982). Mere discussion of public issues or identification as an officeholder on a privately controlled account does not, without more, establish the requisite nexus; Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982), and Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019), caution against converting private editorial control into state action absent delegation of an exclusive public function or coercive governmental involvement. The administrable rule is that blocking is state action only when the account is actually used pursuant to official duty or to exercise governmental authority (e.g., as an official channel for directives, services, or required constituent interaction), not when an employee merely uses a personal page to comment on government matters. Treating every mixed-use account as governmental would chill officials’ private speech and invite pervasive litigation over ordinary online moderation with minimal public benefit.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When an official uses a social-media account as an instrument of governance—holding himself out in his official capacity, disseminating official information, and inviting constituent interaction about public business—his moderation decisions are fairly attributable to the State and thus taken “under color of” state law for § 1983 and the First Amendment. Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the deprivation (blocking/deleting) is attributable to the State where the official’s authority and the account’s function are entwined with his public role, consistent with Brentwood Academy’s emphasis on practical entwinement rather than formal labels. Treating such an account as private simply because it is “personally” owned would permit officials to evade viewpoint-neutrality obligations while exercising de facto governmental communication power, undermining access to public discourse for vulnerable or disfavored speakers. This approach aligns with Davison v. Randall’s recognition that officials who open interactive spaces for constituent engagement on official matters may not exclude critics based on viewpoint under the First Amendment as incorporated via the Fourteenth Amendment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil, the § 1983 “under color of law” inquiry tracks state-action attribution: the question is whether the challenged conduct is fairly attributable to the State, not merely whether the actor holds office. When an official uses a social-media account as an ongoing channel for government communication—holding himself out in his official role, conveying official information, and inviting constituent interaction about city business—moderation decisions (including blocking) are best understood as exercises of official authority in that communicative space, akin to the analyses in Davison and the (mooted) Knight litigation. That rule is workable and textually coherent because it ties First Amendment constraints to the nature of the act performed—communicating and managing an official channel—rather than the private ownership of the device/account, while avoiding overbreadth under Blum and Halleck by not converting every personal account mentioning public issues into state action. On these facts as framed, Freed’s use of the page for constituent-facing official communications makes the blocking decision attributable to the State and thus subject to First Amendment viewpoint-discrimination limits through the Fourteenth Amendment and § 1983.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983 and the First Amendment reach only conduct “under color of” law, meaning the challenged act must be “fairly attributable to the State” and involve a misuse of power “possessed by virtue of state law and made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with the authority of state law.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 924 (1982); Monroe v. Pape, 365 U.S. 167, 184 (1961). On this record as framed, operating and moderating a privately owned social-media account—even while discussing public matters and identifying oneself by title—does not by itself amount to exercising governmental power or performing a duty imposed by law; absent coercion, significant encouragement, or other close nexus, the moderation choice remains private conduct. See Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991, 1004 (1982); Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802, 810–812 (2019). While a different case might show an account formally used as an official channel (e.g., mandated by office or controlled through governmental resources), the Constitution’s limits cannot be extended beyond state action without collapsing the under-color-of-law requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The First Amendment and § 1983 apply only to conduct “fairly attributable to the State,” which under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil requires that the challenged deprivation be caused by the exercise of a right or privilege created by the State or by a person for whom the State is responsible. On this record, respondent’s operation of a privately controlled Facebook page—without a showing that the government delegated him authority to run the page as an official channel, required him to use it, or otherwise exercised control over its moderation—looks more like private conduct that is not transformed into state action merely because he sometimes discussed public issues. Consistent with Halleck and Blum, we should resist expanding state-action doctrine to treat a public employee’s personal speech platform as a government forum absent clear governmental compulsion, delegation, or entwinement. A narrower, more workable rule (state action only when the official uses the account pursuant to actual or apparent governmental authority to speak/act for the State) better preserves judicial restraint and avoids chilling officials’ personal participation in public debate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1983 and the Fourteenth Amendment reach only deprivations “under color of” state law, a limitation that tracks the constitutional requirement that the challenged conduct be “fairly attributable to the State.” Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922, 929, 937 (1982). A public employee’s private use of a privately owned social-media account does not become state action merely because he discusses public issues or identifies his title; the relevant question is whether the specific act of blocking was undertaken in an official capacity or by exercising authority made possible only by state law, rather than ordinary private control over a personal page. See Blum v. Yaretsky, 457 U.S. 991 (1982); Manhattan Cmty. Access Corp. v. Halleck, 587 U.S. 802 (2019). On this record, treating any mixed-use account as governmental would dilute Lugar’s attribution requirement and improperly expand First Amendment constraints to private conduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., the relevant question is whether the challenged blocking is "fairly attributable to the State"—i.e., whether the deprivation was caused by an exercise of authority or responsibility created by state law and undertaken in an official capacity (mirrored by § 1983’s “under color of” requirement). When an official uses a social-media account as an operational channel of governance—holding himself out as City Manager, conveying official information, and inviting constituents’ engagement about city business—his moderation of that interactive space is best understood as the exercise of governmental communicative authority, not merely private curation. Treating such blocking as private conduct would create an easy end-run around First Amendment constraints and invite viewpoint discrimination in a de facto public-facing forum, a practical consequence inconsistent with procedural fairness and equal protection values. This approach aligns with Davison v. Randall and the forum-focused analysis in Knight v. Trump (vacated as moot), while remaining faithful to Halleck’s admonition that state action turns on attribution to the State rather than the mere existence of a platform.
